lab_title: Apparent Retrograde Motion: Solving the Planetary Puzzle
top_level_objectives: Observe the apparent retrograde motion of Mars against the background stars from an Earth-bound perspective.
Contrast the historical geocentric explanation of epicycles with the modern heliocentric model.
Visualize how Earth overtaking a slower outer planet creates an optical illusion of backward motion.
Analyze how a planet's distance from the Sun affects the characteristics of its retrograde loop.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion as observed from Earth over several months.
key_visuals: A realistic night sky scene with the zodiac constellations clearly marked.
A timeline UI showing the progression of days and months.
student_actions: Scrub the timeline forward to watch Mars drift eastward.
Identify the exact date when Mars stops and begins moving westward.
Continue scrubbing to trace the full retrograde loop and normal motion resumption.

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how ancient astronomers explained retrograde motion using complex orbital mechanics.
key_visuals: Earth placed at the center of the system.
Mars attached to a small circular orbit (epicycle) that moves along a larger orbit (deferent) around Earth.
A traced path showing the resulting looping motion.
student_actions: Activate the deferent motion alone to see a simple orbit.
Activate the epicycle motion to observe the combined looping effect.
Evaluate why this model, while mathematically functional, appears physically awkward.

scenes.brief_purpose: Reveal the true cause of retrograde motion by shifting to a top-down view of the solar system.
key_visuals: The Sun at the center with Earth and Mars on their respective orbits.
A dashed line of sight extending from Earth through Mars to a distant star field backdrop.
A projected tracing on the star field showing what an Earth observer sees.
student_actions: Start the orbital simulation and observe Earth moving faster than Mars.
Watch the line of sight indicator as Earth approaches, overtakes, and passes Mars.
Correlate the moment Earth passes Mars with the backward loop drawn on the star field.

scenes.brief_purpose: Connect the abstract astronomical concept to a familiar Earth-bound experience.
key_visuals: A perspective from inside a faster-moving vehicle on a curved multi-lane track.
A slower-moving vehicle in the outer lane.
Distant mountains or buildings serving as a static background.
student_actions: Ride in the inner lane vehicle and observe the slower outer vehicle.
Note how the slower vehicle appears to move backward relative to the distant background as you pass it.
Map the vehicles to Earth and Mars to reinforce the optical illusion concept.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explore how orbital distance influences the visual size and frequency of retrograde loops.
key_visuals: A zoomed-out heliocentric solar system model showing orbits of Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Lines of sight for each outer planet extending to the star field.
Simultaneous tracings of the apparent motion of all three planets.
student_actions: Observe the relative orbital speeds of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Compare the width of Mars's retrograde loop to those of Jupiter and Saturn.
Conclude that planets further from Earth exhibit smaller apparent retrograde loops due to the smaller relative angle change.
